title: Malaysia's power system faces constraints amid high data center demand: Regulator
key_facts: Siti Safinah Salleh, Chief Executive Officer of the Energy Commission (EC), Malaysia's energy regulator, reportedly said at a seminar last week that high data-centre demand is pressuring generation and grid capacity.
Electricity demand growth used to be 1.5 to 2 per cent but is now pushing 10 per cent because of data centres.
Data centres are willing to commit to only 5 to 15 years of electricity demand, while grid investments take about 20 years to recover on a shared basis.
Data centres typically need power in about 18 to 24 months; building a power plant takes more than five years, especially with supply chain constraints.
Bottlenecks exist in places such as Perak, where demand exceeds available capacity even though capacity remains elsewhere.
Malaysia's Corporate Renewable Energy Supply Scheme (CRESS) has a low take-up rate because unused capacity cannot easily be sold back into the system, a data centre operator said.
The CEO listed three issues: supply sufficiency, the speed of infrastructure expansion, and whether investment can be recovered.
quote_evidence: High electricity demand from data centers is putting pressure on Malaysia’s power generation and grid capacity, the country’s energy regulator warns, adding that recovering the investment is proving harder due to the short-term commitments from some operators.
Electricity demand growth used to be 1.5 – 2 per cent but is now pushing 10 per cent due to data centers.
The big mismatch is when data centers are only willing to commit to between 5-15 years of electricity demand when grid investments take about 20 years to recover on a shared basis.
